claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection produced transcriptional changes associated with increased glycolysis and lipid accumulation.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection produced transcriptional changes associated with increased glycolysis and lipid accumulation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis of infected primary cells and patient samples showing enrichment in metabolic processes, particularly glycolysis and lipid metabolism, as well as microscopic and metabolic assays confirming increased glucose uptake, lactate production, and lipid accumulation.

claim: Fenofibrate reversed lipid accumulation and blocked SARS-CoV-2 replication through a PPARα-dependent mechanism in both alpha and delta variants.
source: Metabolism-focused drug screen showed that fenofibrate reversed lipid accumulation and blocked SARS-CoV-2 replication through a PPARα-dependent mechanism in both alpha and delta variants.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro experiments showing fenofibrate reduced phospholipid accumulation and viral load by 2-4 logs in primary lung cells infected with alpha and delta variants, with effects reversed by CPT1A inhibition and PPARα knockout.

claim: Israeli patients taking fibrates showed significantly lower markers of immunoinflammation and faster recovery.
source: Analysis of 3233 Israeli patients hospitalized due to COVID-19 supported in vitro findings. Patients taking fibrates showed significantly lower markers of immunoinflammation and faster recovery.
evidence: Supported by observational data from 3233 Israeli COVID-19 patients showing fibrate users had lower CRP levels, lower NLR, shorter hospitalization duration, and no reported deaths in the small cohort.

claim: Patients receiving fenofibrate demonstrated a rapid reduction in inflammation and a significantly faster recovery compared to patients admitted during the same period.
source: Patients receiving fenofibrate demonstrated a rapid reduction in inflammation and a significantly faster recovery compared to patients admitted during the same period.
evidence: Supported by interventional study data showing fenofibrate-treated patients had significantly lower CRP levels by day 3-5, lower NLR, shorter hospitalization (HR: 3.6, 95% CI 2.1-6.4, p<0.001), and higher oxygen withdrawal rates.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has infected over 265 million individuals worldwide, causing nearly 5.3 million deaths since its emergence.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has infected over 265 million individuals worldwide, causing nearly 5.3 million deaths since its emergence.
evidence: This is a factual statement about epidemiological data that would be based on established public health records and reporting systems at the time of manuscript writing.

claim: Elevated blood glucose, obesity, and hyperlipidemia were found to be risk factors for SARS-CoV-2-induced acute respiratory distress, independently from diabetes.
source: Elevated blood glucose, obesity, and hyperlipidemia were found to be risk factors for SARS-CoV-2-induced acute respiratory distress, independently from diabetes (Bornstein et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Bornstein et al., 2020 and Zhu et al., 2020b.

claim: Metabolic risk factors are associated with a more than 3-fold increase in COVID-19 severity risk.
source: In fact, metabolic risk factors are associated with a more than 3-fold increase in COVID-19 severity risk, whereas inflammatory lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthma are associated with less than a 1.5-fold increase in risk (Ko et al., 2020; Williamson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Ko et al., 2020 and Williamson et al., 2020.

claim: Inflammatory lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthma are associated with less than a 1.5-fold increase in COVID-19 severity risk.
source: In fact, metabolic risk factors are associated with a more than 3-fold increase in COVID-19 severity risk, whereas inflammatory lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthma are associated with less than a 1.5-fold increase in risk (Ko et al., 2020; Williamson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Ko et al., 2020 and Williamson et al., 2020.

claim: Metabolomics of COVID-19 patient sera showed alterations in circulating amino acids, glucose, and lipids, correlated with changes in inflammation and renal function.
source: Metabolomics of COVID-19 patient sera showed alterations in circulating amino acids, glucose, and lipids, correlated with changes in inflammation and renal function (Thomas et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Thomas et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infected monocytes showed raised glycolysis.
source: Work on SARS-CoV-2 infected monocytes showed raised glycolysis (Codo et al., 2020; Ajaz et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Codo et al., 2020 and Ajaz et al., 2021.

claim: Proteomics of infected kidney and colon cells showed that SARS-CoV-2 proteins interact with mitochondria, glycolysis, and lipid metabolism.
source: whereas proteomics of infected kidney and colon cells showed that SARS-CoV-2 proteins interact with mitochondria, glycolysis, and lipid metabolism (Gordon et al., 2020; Bojkova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Gordon et al., 2020 and Bojkova et al., 2020.

claim: Transcriptional analyses showed SARS-CoV-2 induced significant changes in metabolic pathways.
source: Other transcriptional analyses showed SARS-CoV-2 induced significant changes in similar metabolic pathways (Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021; Islam and Khan, 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Delorey et al., 2021; Melms et al., 2021; Islam and Khan, 2020; Singh et al., 2021.

claim: SARS and MERS infections are reliant on altered lipid metabolism.
source: These results support earlier observations that the closely related SARS and MERS infections are reliant on altered lipid metabolism (Yuan et al., 2019; McBride and Machamer, 2010; Yan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Yuan et al., 2019; McBride and Machamer, 2010; Yan et al., 2019.

claim: Recent clinical studies show conflicting results regarding the role of triglycerides in COVID-19 progression.
source: However, recent clinical studies show conflicting results regarding the role of triglycerides in COVID-19 progression (Barberis et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Masana et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Barberis et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Masana et al., 2021.

claim: Critical differences in lipid metabolism exist between humans and rodents.
source: However, recent clinical studies show conflicting results regarding the role of triglycerides in COVID-19 progression (Barberis et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Masana et al., 2021). While these data suggest that lipid metabolic interventions should be studied in the context of COVID-19, the current reliance on animal experiments limits such efforts due to critical differences in lipid metabolism between humans and rodents (Bergen and Mersmann, 2005; Demetrius, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Bergen and Mersmann, 2005; Demetrius, 2005.

claim: MERS infection was associated with long-term immune dysregulation and enhanced susceptibility to metabolic diseases.
source: MERS infection was associated with long-term immune dysregulation and enhanced susceptibility to metabolic diseases (Kulcsar et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Kulcsar et al., 2019.

claim: SARS infection was associated with long-term alterations in lipid metabolism, hyperlipidemia, and hyperglycemia even 12 years post-recovery.
source: while SARS infection was associated with long-term alterations in lipid metabolism, hyperlipidemia, and hyperglycemia even 12 years post-recovery (Wu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Wu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2010.

claim: Recent work points to similar post-sequelae effects of COVID-19.
source: Recent work points to similar post-sequelae effects of COVID-19 (Akter et al., 2020; Al-Aly et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Akter et al., 2020; Al-Aly et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis of infected primary cells identified 535 differentially expressed genes (FDR <0.05).
source: RNA-Seq analysis of infected primary cells identified 535 differentially expressed genes (FDR <0.05).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis performed on SARS-CoV-2 infected primary human bronchial epithelial cells.

claim: Enrichment analysis identified the regulation of viral transcription (FDR <3 × 10–2), immune processes (FDR <9 × 10–4), and cellular response to stress (FDR <5 × 10–11) in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: Enrichment analysis identified the regulation of viral transcription (FDR <3 × 10–2), immune processes (FDR <9 × 10–4), and cellular response to stress (FDR <5 × 10–11).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes from RNA-Seq data.

claim: All four sample groups showed significant enrichment in metabolic processes (FDR <4 × 10–4), particularly lipid (FDR <2 × 10–5) and carbohydrate metabolic processes (FDR <0.05).
source: These four sample groups also display significant enrichment in metabolic processes (FDR <4 × 10–4), particularly lipid (FDR <2 × 10–5) and carbohydrate metabolic processes (FDR <0.05; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data from four different sample groups (bronchial culture, small airway culture, autopsy, and lavage) as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Across all four sample groups 58 ± 3% of the differentially expressed genes were metabolism-related, with 15 ± 2% of the genes associated with lipid metabolism.
source: Across all four sample groups 58 ± 3% of the differentially expressed genes were metabolism-related, with 15 ± 2% of the genes associated with lipid metabolism.
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1B comparing differentially expressed genes with metabolic and lipid metabolism gene sets.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection induced key glycolysis genes including rate-limiting enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2) and pyruvate kinase isozyme (PKM).
source: Mapping differentially expressed genes on the central carbon metabolism pathway showed that SARS-CoV-2 induces key glycolysis genes (Figure 1D) including rate-limiting enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2) and pyruvate kinase isozyme (PKM).
evidence: Supported by gene expression mapping on metabolic pathways shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) was up-regulated suggesting a shift toward fatty acid synthesis.
source: Interestingly, while core genes of the citric acid cycle did not change significantly, ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) was up-regulated suggesting a shift toward fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing differential expression of ACLY gene.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection induced HMG-CoA synthase (HMGCS) and squalene monooxygenase (SQLE), rate-limiting steps in cholesterol synthesis.
source: Mapping of differentially expressed genes on lipid metabolism (Figure 1D) showed induction of HMG-CoA synthase (HMGCS) and squalene monooxygenase (SQLE), rate-limiting steps in cholesterol synthesis (Sharpe and Brown, 2013).
evidence: Supported by gene expression mapping shown in Figure 1D and citation to Sharpe and Brown, 2013 for the role of these enzymes in cholesterol synthesis.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection showed significant down-regulation of lipid catabolism genes CPT1A and ACSL1 (n=3, FDR <0.01).
source: Surprisingly, we found only a few significantly up-regulated lipogenesis genes, but rather significant down-regulation of lipid catabolism genes CPT1A and ACSL1 (n=3, FDR <0.01) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis showing differential expression of CPT1A and ACSL1 genes with statistical significance (n=3, FDR <0.01).

claim: Microscopic analysis showed an 85% increase in intracellular glucose in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: Microscopic analysis showed an 85% increase in intracellular glucose in infected cells (Figure 1E; methods).
evidence: Supported by microscopic evaluation using fluorescent glucose analog (2-NDBG) shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Metabolic analysis showed a 50% increase (n=6, p<0.001) in lactate production in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: Concurrent metabolic analysis showed a 50% increase (n=6, <0.001) in lactate production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by direct metabolic measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glycolytic index shifted from 1 to 1.7 indicating a Warburg-like effect in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: and a shift in the lactate over glucose ratio (glycolytic index) from 1 to 1.7 indicating a Warburg-like effect (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by calculation of lactate to glucose ratio from metabolic measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy showed an increase of neutral lipids (n=3, p<0.05) and a significant accumulation of phospholipids (n=3, p<0.001) in SARS-CoV-2 infected primary lung cells.
source: Alterations in lipid metabolism were confirmed by fluorescence microscopy, showing an increase of neutral lipids (n=3, p<0.05) and a significant accumulation of phospholipids (n=3, p<0.001) in SARS-CoV-2 infected primary lung cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy using lipid staining shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection of primary cells induced the dsRNA-activated protein kinase R (PKR/PERK) and IRE1 pathways leading to differential expression of ATF4 and splicing of XBP1.
source: Indeed, SARS-CoV-2 infection of primary cells induced the dsRNA-activated protein kinase R (PKR/PERK) and IRE1 pathways leading to differential expression of ATF4 and splicing of XBP1.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis of ER stress pathway genes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATF6 pathway of ER stress was seemingly unaffected by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The ATF6 pathway of ER stress was seemingly unaffected by infection.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis showing no significant changes in ATF6 pathway genes.

claim: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to a Warburg-like shift to anaerobic glycolysis.
source: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to a Warburg-like shift to anaerobic glycolysis (Yu et al., 2014), increased lipogenesis (Han and Kaufman, 2016; Yu et al., 2013), and decreased lipid catabolism (Rutkowski et al., 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Yu et al., 2014; Han and Kaufman, 2016; Yu et al., 2013; Rutkowski et al., 2008.

claim: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to increased lipogenesis.
source: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to a Warburg-like shift to anaerobic glycolysis (Yu et al., 2014), increased lipogenesis (Han and Kaufman, 2016; Yu et al., 2013), and decreased lipid catabolism (Rutkowski et al., 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Han and Kaufman, 2016; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to decreased lipid catabolism.
source: Induction of PKR/PERK and IRE1 pathways were previously shown to lead to a Warburg-like shift to anaerobic glycolysis (Yu et al., 2014), increased lipogenesis (Han and Kaufman, 2016; Yu et al., 2013), and decreased lipid catabolism (Rutkowski et al., 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Rutkowski et al., 2008.

claim: Microscopic analysis showed involvement of viral proteins N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 in glucose accumulation (n=6).
source: Microscopic analysis of intracellular glucose retention showed the involvement of a small subset of viral proteins including N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 in glucose accumulation (n=6; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by microscopic analysis of primary cells expressing individual viral proteins shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Direct measurement showed a marked increase in lactate production in cells expressing viral proteins N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 (n=6, p<0.01).
source: Direct measurement of glucose uptake and lactate production showed a marked increase in lactate production in cells expressing the same viral protein subset (n=6, p<0.01; Figure 2B) confirming a viral protein-driven shift to glycolysis (n=6, p<0.01; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by direct sensor measurements of lactate in cells expressing viral proteins shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Seahorse analysis confirmed increased glycolysis induced by viral proteins N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 (n=6).
source: Independent measurement of extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), a surrogate measurement for glycolysis (Mookerjee et al., 2017), confirmed the activity of these viral proteins (n=6; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse ECAR measurements shown in Figure 2D and citation to Mookerjee et al., 2017 for the methodology.

claim: Mitochondrial stress test analysis showed a marked disruption in oxidative phosphorylation, induced by expression of N, ORF3a, and NSP7 (n=6, p<0.05).
source: Mitochondrial stress test analysis (methods) showed a marked disruption in oxidative phosphorylation, induced by expression of N, ORF3a, and NSP7 (n=6, p<0.05; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse mitochondrial stress test measurements shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Seahorse fatty acid oxidation analysis showed marked disruption in fatty acid oxidation, induced by expression of ORF9c, M, N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 (n=4, p<0.05).
source: To study the role of viral proteins in lipid metabolism, we measured the exogenous fatty acid oxidation using Seahorse (methods) showing marked disruption in fatty acid oxidation, induced by expression of ORF9c, M, N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 (n=4, p<0.05; Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse fatty acid oxidation measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Microscopic analysis confirmed a significant accumulation of phospholipids induced by expression of viral proteins ORF9c, M, N, ORF3a, NSP7, ORF8, NSP5, and NSP12 (n=6, p<0.01).
source: While triglyceride accumulation did not change, microscopic analysis confirmed a significant accumulation of phospholipids induced by expression of the same viral proteins (n=6, p<0.01; Figure 2F) supporting the significance of lipid accumulation for SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy of lipid accumulation in cells expressing viral proteins shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The inhibition of lipid catabolism by SARS-CoV-2 infection is a unique host response compared to other viral infections.
source: The inhibition of lipid catabolism by SARS-CoV-2 infection of primary lung epithelial cells and associated lipid accumulation is a unique host response (Levy et al., 2016) that might offer a distinct metabolic intervention.
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous work on other viruses cited as Levy et al., 2016.

claim: Fibrates and other metabolic interventions that increase lipid catabolism might interfere with the SARS-CoV-2 lifecycle.
source: These data suggest that fibrates and other metabolic interventions that increase lipid catabolism (Lalloyer and Staels, 2010; Fruchart and Duriez, 2006) and reduce inflammatory stress (Bocher et al., 2001; Sheu et al., 2002; Price et al., 2012; Ann et al., 2015) might interfere with the virus lifecycle.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed metabolic changes and known effects of fibrates, supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Fibrates increase lipid catabolism.
source: These data suggest that fibrates and other metabolic interventions that increase lipid catabolism (Lalloyer and Staels, 2010; Fruchart and Duriez, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Lalloyer and Staels, 2010; Fruchart and Duriez, 2006.

claim: Fibrates reduce inflammatory stress.
source: and reduce inflammatory stress (Bocher et al., 2001; Sheu et al., 2002; Price et al., 2012; Ann et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Bocher et al., 2001; Sheu et al., 2002; Price et al., 2012; Ann et al., 2015.

claim: Pharmacological modulation of host metabolism was shown to block replication in other viruses.
source: Pharmacological modulation of host metabolism was shown to block replication in other viruses (Levy et al., 2016; Gualdoni et al., 2018; Kilbourne, 1959; Fujita et al., 2006; Ikeda et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Levy et al., 2016; Gualdoni et al., 2018; Kilbourne, 1959; Fujita et al., 2006; Ikeda et al., 2006.

claim: Metformin can modulate mitochondrial activity potentially reversing a Warburg-like effect.
source: SGLT inhibitors can block glucose absorption, while metformin can modulate mitochondrial activity potentially reversing a Warburg-like effect (Andrzejewski et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Andrzejewski et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2018.

claim: Telmisartan could act by decreasing ER stress through IRE1 inhibition.
source: Telmisartan could act by decreasing ER stress through IRE1 inhibition (Tong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Tong et al., 2016.

claim: Thiazolidinediones are PPARγ agonists that modulate lipid content in certain tissues and are thought to reduce lung inflammation.
source: Thiazolidinediones are PPARγ agonists that modulate lipid content in certain tissues and are thought to reduce lung inflammation (Ahmadian et al., 2013; Belvisi and Mitchell, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Ahmadian et al., 2013; Belvisi and Mitchell, 2009.

claim: Cells treated with PPARα agonist fenofibrate showed a significant decrease in phospholipid content (n=3, p<0.001).
source: Cells treated with PPARα agonist fenofibrate showed a significant decrease in phospholipid content (n=3, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by microscopic analysis of lipid accumulation in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells treated with fenofibrate shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fenofibrate significantly reduced the lactate-to-glucose ratio by 60% (n=3; p<0.01) normalizing the metabolic shift induced by infection.
source: Fenofibrate significantly reduced the lactate-to-glucose ratio by 60% (n=3; p<0.01) normalizing the metabolic shift induced by infection.
evidence: Supported by metabolic measurements of lactate and glucose in fenofibrate-treated infected cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate (Cmax) reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 2-logs (n=3; p<0.001).
source: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate (Cmax) reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 2-logs (n=3; p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in fenofibrate-treated cells shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM cloperastine reduced viral load by 2.5–3-fold (n=3; p<0.05).
source: Treatment with 10 µM cloperastine reduced viral load by 2.5–3-fold (n=3; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in cloperastine-treated cells shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cell number post-treatment was unaffected by all drugs tested (n=3).
source: Cell number post-treatment was unaffected by all drugs tested. (n=3).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assessment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All four PPARα agonists showed a similar effect in both alpha and delta strains of the virus, blocking phospholipid accumulation (n=6, p<0.05).
source: All four PPARα agonists showed a similar effect in both alpha and delta strains of the virus (method), blocking phospholipid accumulation (n=6, p<0.05; Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by microscopic analysis of lipid accumulation in cells infected with alpha and delta variants and treated with different PPARα agonists shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate, 50 µM bezafibrate, or 1 µM WY-14643 reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 3–5-logs (n=6; p<0.001).
source: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate, 50 µM bezafibrate, or 1 µM WY-14643 reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 3–5-logs (n=6; p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in cells treated with different PPARα agonists shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Treatment with 50 µM conjugated (9Z,11E)-linoleic acid and 50 µM oleic acid reduced viral load by 2.5-logs (n=6; p<0.01 in alpha variant).
source: Treatment with 50 µM conjugated (9Z,11E)-linoleic acid and 50 µM oleic acid reduced viral load by 2.5-logs (n=6; p<0.01 in alpha variant).
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in cells treated with conjugated linoleic acid shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Cells treated with fenofibrate showed a significant decrease in phospholipid content in both alpha and delta viruses (n=6, p<0.001), which was reversed by the addition of etomoxir.
source: Cells treated with fenofibrate showed a significant decrease in phospholipid content in both viruses (n=6, p<0.001). Phospholipid decrease was reversed by the addition of etomoxir.
evidence: Supported by microscopic analysis of lipid accumulation in infected cells treated with fenofibrate with or without etomoxir shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 4–5-logs (n=6; p<0.001), and this antiviral effect was reversed by the addition of etomoxir.
source: Treatment with 20 µM fenofibrate reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral load by 4–5-logs (n=6; p<0.001). Fenofibrate antiviral effect was reversed by the addition of etomoxir.
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in cells treated with fenofibrate with or without etomoxir shown in Figure 3I.

claim: PPARα CRISPR-knockout cells treated with fenofibrate did not show a decrease in phospholipid content in either virus and was unaffected by etomoxir (n=6).
source: PPARα or NT CRISPR-knockout cells treated with fenofibrate did not show a decrease in phospholipid content in either virus and was unaffected by etomoxir (n=6).
evidence: Supported by microscopic analysis of lipid accumulation in PPARα knockout cells treated with fenofibrate shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Genetic inhibition of PPARα causes cells to be refractory to fenofibrate treatment and the addition of etomoxir (n=6).
source: Genetic inhibition of PPARα causes cells to be refractory to fenofibrate treatment and the addition of etomoxir (n=6).
evidence: Supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of viral RNA in PPARα knockout cells treated with fenofibrate shown in Figure 3K.

claim: PPARα-dependent fatty acid oxidation inhibits the proliferation of SARS-CoV-2 in primary lung epithelial cells.
source: Together, these data suggest that PPARα-dependent fatty acid oxidation inhibits the proliferation of SARS-CoV-2 in primary lung epithelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from experiments with PPARα agonists, CPT1A inhibition, and PPARα knockout.

claim: A total of 3233 cases of confirmed COVID-19 patients were admitted to Hadassah and Ichilov Medical Centers between March 2020 to February 2021.
source: To assess the clinical relevance of these findings we collected a total of 3233 cases of confirmed COVID-19 patients admitted to Hadassah and Ichilov Medical Centers between March 2020 to February 2021.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the observational study cohort.

claim: A total of 1156 of these patients (35.8%) were registered with in-hospital use of different metabolic regulators.
source: A total of 1156 of these patients (35.8%) were registered with in-hospital use of different metabolic regulators (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the observational study cohort.

claim: Participants treated with metabolic regulators were older and had a higher prevalence of chronic medical conditions than those without these treatments.
source: Participants treated with metabolic regulators were older and had a higher prevalence of chronic medical conditions, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, and chronic kidney diseases than those without these treatments (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by demographic and clinical characteristics data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Patients taking thiazolidinediones (n=37; p<0.001), metformin (n=321; p<0.01), SGLT2 inhibitors (n=54; p<0.001), statins (n=924; p<0.001), or telmisartan (n=278; p<0.001) were over-represented across all severity indicators.
source: Comparison between 2806 COVID-19 patients above the age of 30 and 532,493 recent unique hospital patient records showed a significant over-representation of patients taking thiazolidinediones, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, statins, or telmisartan (IRE1α inhibitor) across all COVID-19 severity indicators (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of COVID-19 patients versus general hospital records shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Patients taking fibrates (n=21) were significantly underrepresented in hospital admissions (p=0.02) and not over-represented in other severity indicators.
source: However, patients taking fibrates (n=21) were significantly underrepresented in hospital admissions (p=0.02) and not over-represented in other severity indicators (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of COVID-19 patients versus general hospital records shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Israeli patients taking bezafibrate or ciprofibrate (fibrates) were associated with significantly lower hospitalization duration (p=0.03).
source: In general, fibrates use was associated with significantly shorter hospitalization duration (p=0.03; Figure 4B,Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of hospitalization duration in fibrate users shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Patients taking fibrates showed a significant decline in inflammation within 5 days post-admission.
source: Importantly, patients taking fibrates showed a significant decline in inflammation within 5 days post-admission (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by dynamic tracking of CRP levels shown in Figure 4C using Lowess smoothing.

claim: Patients taking fibrates showed consistently low NLR throughout their hospitalization, suggesting minimal immunoinflammatory stress.
source: However, patients taking fibrates showed consistently low NLR throughout their hospitalization, suggesting minimal immunoinflammatory stress.
evidence: Supported by dynamic tracking of NLR shown in Figure 4D using Lowess smoothing.

claim: No deaths were reported for the small group of patients taking fibrates (n=16).
source: Analysis of 28-day all-cause mortality showed that no deaths were reported for the small group of patients taking fibrates (n=16, Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mortality was significantly higher in patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors (aHR = 2.6; 95% CI, 1.1–6.2; p=0.034) or thiazolidinedione (aHR = 3.6; 95% CI, 1.0–12.4; p=0.043).
source: Mortality did not appear to differ for statins, IRE1α inhibitors, or metformin, but was significantly higher in patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors (aHR = 2.6; 95% CI, 1.1–6.2; p=0.034) or thiazolidinedione (aHR = 3.6; 95% CI, 1.0–12.4; p=0.043; Figure 4E; Supplementary file 2; methods).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis of 28-day mortality shown in Figure 4E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Fenofibrate users regardless of additional treatment had significantly less COVID-19 history and severe illness in the Italian cohort.
source: Analysis of an additional observational cohort of 2123 patients examined in the Outpatient Lipid Clinics of the University of Bologna and the Niguarda Hospital in Milan during the last 12 months and on adequately dosed statins, fenofibrate, or both for at least 3 months (Supplementary file 3) indicates that fenofibrate users regardless of additional treatment had significantly less COVID-19 history and severe illness (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Italian observational cohort data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the Italian sub-cohort of patients reporting contact with affected people, statin users are significantly more likely to develop COVID-19 (p=0.02).
source: Additionally, in the sub-cohort of patients reporting contact with affected people, analysis indicates that statin users are significantly more likely to develop COVID-19 (p=0.02), while fenofibrate users, regardless of additional treatment are less likely to develop COVID-19 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Italian observational cohort data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the Italian sub-cohort of patients reporting contact with affected people, fenofibrate users are less likely to develop COVID-19.
source: Additionally, in the sub-cohort of patients reporting contact with affected people, analysis indicates that statin users are significantly more likely to develop COVID-19 (p=0.02), while fenofibrate users, regardless of additional treatment are less likely to develop COVID-19 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Italian observational cohort data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the US VHA cohort, fenofibrate users have shorter hospitalization duration.
source: Parallel analysis of an observational cohort of 920,922 veterans with hypertension in the US Veteran's Health Administration, comparing fenofibrate to matched non-users, statins users, or thiazolidinediones users (VHA; Supplementary file 3), showed that fenofibrate users have shorter hospitalization duration (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: Supported by analysis of US VHA observational cohort data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the US VHA cohort, fenofibrate users have fairly better outcomes across several severity indicators.
source: and fairly better outcomes across several severity indicators (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of US VHA observational cohort data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Fifteen patients with severe COVID-19 were treated with 145 mg/day of nanocrystallized fenofibrate added to standard-of-care for 10 days or until discharge.
source: Fifteen patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 4) were treated with 145 mg/day of nanocrystallized fenofibrate added to standard-of-care for 10 days or until discharge (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is a factual statement about the interventional study design.

claim: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate has improved lung bioavailability.
source: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate was selected due to its improved lung bioavailability (Chapman, 1987) and short Tmax (Ling et al., 2013; Maciejewski and Hilleman, 2008) enabling rapid intervention (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Chapman, 1987; Ling et al., 2013; Maciejewski and Hilleman, 2008.

claim: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate has a short Tmax enabling rapid intervention.
source: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate was selected due to its improved lung bioavailability (Chapman, 1987) and short Tmax (Ling et al., 2013; Maciejewski and Hilleman, 2008) enabling rapid intervention (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Ling et al., 2013; Maciejewski and Hilleman, 2008.

claim: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate had a significantly lower hospitalization duration (n=15, p<0.001).
source: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate had a significantly lower hospitalization duration (n=15, p<0.001), and a higher likelihood of discharge (HR: 3.6, 95% CI 2.1–6.4, n=15, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by analysis of hospitalization duration and Cox regression shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate had a higher likelihood of discharge (HR: 3.6, 95% CI 2.1–6.4, n=15, p<0.001).
source: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate had a significantly lower hospitalization duration (n=15, p<0.001), and a higher likelihood of discharge (HR: 3.6, 95% CI 2.1–6.4, n=15, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate-treated patients showed a faster decline in inflammation, resulting in significantly lower CRP levels 3–5 days post-treatment (n=15, p<0.001).
source: Nanocrystallized fenofibrate-treated patients showed a faster decline in inflammation, resulting in significantly lower CRP levels 3–5 days post-treatment (n=15, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by dynamic tracking of CRP levels shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate showed no increase in NLR, suggesting minimal immune response, resulting in a significantly lower NLR 3–5 days post-treatment (n=15; p=0.002).
source: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate showed no increase in NLR, suggesting minimal immune response, resulting in a significantly lower NLR 3–5 days post-treatment (n=15; p=0.002).
evidence: Supported by dynamic tracking of NLR shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Patients treated with fenofibrate showed significantly increased withdrawal rate from supplemental oxygen by day 7 (weighted difference of 26.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 7.0–45.2; p=0.003).
source: Patients treated with nanocrystallized fenofibrate also exhibited lower mortality, lower respiratory intervention rates, and significantly increased withdrawal rate from supplemental oxygen by day 7 (weighed difference of 26.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 7.0–45.2; p=0.003; Figure 5F; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of oxygen withdrawal shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Novaplex SARS-CoV-2 variant analysis showed a dominant presence of 69/70 deletion and N501Y substitution mutation correlating to the B.1.1.7 (UK) variant in the patient population.
source: Novaplex SARS-CoV-2 variant analysis showed a dominant presence of 69/70 deletion and N501Y substitution mutation correlating to the B.1.1.7 (UK) variant of the virus in the patient population (Figure 5H)
evidence: Supported by variant detection analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Only one patient suffered from respiratory symptoms and fatigue 6 months post-admission (IR 6.67; 95% CI, 0.1–32.0), without any additional post-acute sequelae in any of the other patients.
source: Investigation into post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 in these patients, 6 months post-admission, revealed that only one patient suffered from respiratory symptoms and fatigue (IR 6.67; 95% CI, 0.1–32.0), without any additional post-acute sequelae in any of the other patients (Figure 5I; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by 6-month follow-up data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Glycolysis is often upregulated to supply nucleotides for virus replication.
source: Glycolysis is often upregulated to supply nucleotides for virus replication (Levy et al., 2016; Gualdoni et al., 2018; Smallwood et al., 2017), as part of a Warburg-like effect.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Levy et al., 2016; Gualdoni et al., 2018; Smallwood et al., 2017.

claim: Recent work in Vero and Caco-2 cell lines showed direct binding of some viral proteins to mitochondrial and glycolysis-related proteins.
source: Recent work in Vero and Caco-2 cell lines, showed direct binding of some viral proteins to mitochondrial and glycolysis-related proteins (Gordon et al., 2020; Bojkova et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Gordon et al., 2020; Bojkova et al., 2020.

claim: Electron microscopy studies confirmed mitochondrial disruption in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: with electron microscopy studies confirming mitochondrial disruption (Zhu et al., 2020c)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Zhu et al., 2020c.

claim: PET-CT studies revealed increased glycolytic activity in lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: and PET-CT studies revealing increased glycolytic activity in lungs of COVID-19 patients (Setti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Setti et al., 2020.

claim: 2-Deoxyglucose (2-DG) blocked SARS-CoV-2 replication, but at concentrations 20-fold higher than Cmax while causing cellular damage.
source: For example, 2-Deoxyglucose (2-DG) blocked SARS-CoV-2 replication, but at concentrations 20-fold higher than Cmax while causing cellular damage (Bojkova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Bojkova et al., 2020.

claim: Recent observational studies support findings that metformin has minimal effect on COVID-19 outcomes.
source: Recent observational studies support our findings (Cheng et al., 2020; Turabian, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Cheng et al., 2020; Turabian, 2020.

claim: Histological analysis of COVID-19 patient biopsies showed enlarged lung epithelial cells with amphophilic granular cytoplasm.
source: Histological analysis of COVID-19 patient biopsies confirms our findings, showing enlarged lung epithelial cells with amphophilic granular cytoplasm (Xu et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Xu et al., 2020.

claim: Electron microscopy images of infected cells showed lipid droplet accumulation.
source: while electron microscopy images of infected cells showed lipid droplet accumulation (Zhu et al., 2020c; Pizzorno et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Zhu et al., 2020c; Pizzorno et al., 2020.

claim: Lipogenesis is poorly tolerated in thin epithelial tissue and might lead to pulmonary lipotoxicity.
source: As lipogenesis is poorly tolerated in thin epithelial tissue, it might lead to pulmonary lipotoxicity (Plantier et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Plantier et al., 2012.

claim: Triacsin C and VPS34 inhibitors blocked viral replication at concentrations 1000-fold higher than Cmax.
source: Triacsin C and VPS34 inhibitors blocked viral replication at concentrations 1000-fold higher than Cmax (Silvas et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Silvas et al., 2020.

claim: Statins showed antiviral effects at concentrations 100-fold higher than Cmax.
source: with similar effects shown for statins at concentrations 100-fold higher than Cmax (Zhang et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Zhang et al., 2020b.

claim: Observational studies on the effect of statins show an inconsistent reduction of 28 days all-cause-mortality and mixed effect regarding secondary outcomes.
source: This gap might explain why observational studies on the effect of statins show an inconsistent reduction of 28 days all-cause-mortality and mixed effect regarding secondary outcomes (Zhang et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Zhang et al., 2020a.

claim: Fibrates are a family of amphipathic carboxylic acids that are ligands of PPARα, known to up-regulate lipid oxidation and lower serum triglycerides.
source: Fibrates are a family of amphipathic carboxylic acids that are ligands of PPARα, known to up-regulate lipid oxidation and lower serum triglycerides (Lalloyer and Staels, 2010; Fruchart and Duriez, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Lalloyer and Staels, 2010; Fruchart and Duriez, 2006.

claim: Fibrates have been shown to produce an anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effect in multiple tissues.
source: Fibrates have also been shown to produce an anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effect in multiple tissues (Bocher et al., 2001; Sheu et al., 2002; Price et al., 2012; Ann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Bocher et al., 2001; Sheu et al., 2002; Price et al., 2012; Ann et al., 2015.

claim: Fenofibrate inhibits viral replication in primary human lung cells at 20 µM concentration, lower than its effective physiological concentration (Cmax) recorded as 25–30 µM with a standard dose of 145 mg/day.
source: We show that fenofibrate inhibits viral replication in primary human lung cells, reversing phospholipid accumulation at 20 µM concentration (Figure 3), lower than its effective physiological concentration (Cmax) recorded as 25–30 µM with a standard dose of 145 mg/day (Wei, 2004; Godfrey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by in vitro data and citations to published studies by Wei, 2004; Godfrey et al., 2011.

claim: Fenofibrate was detected at an effective plasma concentration of 15–20 µM range hours after administration.
source: Fenofibrate was detected at an effective plasma concentration of 15–20 µM range hours after administration (Sonet et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Sonet et al., 2002.

claim: Recent work suggested that fenofibrate might also block viral entry receptors.
source: Recent work suggested that fenofibrate might also block viral entry receptors (Davies et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Davies et al., 2021b.

claim: Cell lines show differences in PPARα expression and activity compared to primary cells and tissue.
source: One challenge in the investigation of host metabolic pathways in vitro is the difficulty to study lipid metabolism in proliferating cell lines and stem-cell-derived models (Levy et al., 2016; Alsabeeh et al., 2018), that in addition to the Warburg effect, also show differences in PPARα expression and activity compared to primary cells and tissue (Uhlén et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 2008; Karlsson et al., 2021; Uhlen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Levy et al., 2016; Alsabeeh et al., 2018; Uhlén et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 2008; Karlsson et al., 2021; Uhlen et al., 2019.

claim: Differences in cell lines result in an effective concentration above clinical relevance, at sub-millimolar ranges.
source: These differences result in an effective concentration above clinical relevance, at sub-millimolar ranges (Davies et al., 2021b), far above the levels tested in standard high content screens (Riva et al., 2020; Bakowski et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Davies et al., 2021b; Riva et al., 2020; Bakowski et al., 2021.

claim: In primary cell cultures, significant cell death is not observed even after 5 days, while the virus is clearly still replicating at this point.
source: In contrast to cell lines, we do not observe significant cell death in primary cell cultures even after 5 days, while the virus is clearly still replicating at this point (Figure 3). This is consistent with other studies in primary tissue and clinical data (Liu et al., 2021; Rosa et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citations to published studies by Liu et al., 2021; Rosa et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020a.

claim: Hamster models are unresponsive to fibrates.
source: One challenge in the validation of our findings is that hamster models are unresponsive to fibrates (Guo et al., 2001; Srivastava and He, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies by Guo et al., 2001; Srivastava and He, 2010.

claim: Thiazolidinediones are ligands of PPARγ that upregulate lipogenesis in certain tissues.
source: Thiazolidinediones are ligands of PPARγ that upregulate lipogenesis in certain tissues (Ahmadian et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Ahmadian et al., 2013.

claim: Long-term thiazolidinedione use is associated with an increased risk of pneumonia in patients with type 2 diabetes.
source: These results correlate with recent data showing that long-term thiazolidinedione use is associated with an increased risk of pneumonia in patients with type 2 diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study by Singh et al., 2011.

claim: Severe COVID-19 patients treated with 145 mg/day of nanocrystallized fenofibrate showed dramatic improvement in inflammation and faster recovery compared to patients admitted during the same period in neighboring hospitals and treated with the same standard of care.
source: Severe COVID-19 patients treated with 145 mg/day of nanocrystallized fenofibrate in addition to standard-of-care showed dramatic improvement in inflammation and faster recovery compared to patients admitted during the same period in neighboring hospitals and treated with the same standard of care (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by interventional study data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patients treated with fenofibrate showed significantly decreased CRP levels 72 hr post-treatment suggesting a rapid decrease in inflammation, possibly due to PPARα anti-inflammatory effect.
source: Patients treated with fenofibrate showed significantly decreased CRP levels 72 hr post-treatment suggesting a rapid decrease in inflammation, possibly due to PPARα anti-inflammatory effect.
evidence: Supported by CRP tracking data from the interventional study.

claim: In a 6-month follow-up, fenofibrate-treated patients report post-acute sequelae far below the rates reported in the literature.
source: In a 6-month follow-up, these patients report post-acute sequelae far below the rates reported in the literature (Al-Aly et al., 2021; Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by 6-month follow-up data shown in Figure 5I and comparison to published study by Al-Aly et al., 2021.

claim: Baseline differences between the groups and lack of randomization in the interventional study mean that confounding and/or random error cannot be excluded.
source: While our clinical results are highly encouraging, baseline differences between the groups and lack of randomization must be noted. Therefore, confounding and/or random error cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: The higher comorbidity burden in the fenofibrate group may have conditioned a lower threshold for the initial hospital admission, with consequent favorable differences in outcomes relative to controls.
source: For instance, the higher comorbidity burden in the fenofibrate group may have conditioned a lower threshold for the initial hospital admission, with consequent favorable differences in outcomes relative to controls.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential confounding factors.

claim: Standard of care during the study time period was identical for all clinical centers in Israel.
source: Standard of care during this time period was identical for all clinical centers in Israel.
evidence: This is a factual statement about clinical practice during the study period.

claim: Two randomized placebo-controlled trials of fenofibrate for COVID-19 are ongoing, including a large international trial in the US, Mexico, Greece, and several South American countries (FERMIN trial; NCT04517396), and a clinical trial in Israel (FENOC trial; NCT04661930).
source: Two randomized placebo-controlled trials are ongoing, including a large international trial in the US, Mexico, Greece, and several South American countries (FERMIN trial; NCT04517396), and a clinical trial in Israel (FENOC trial; NCT04661930).
evidence: This is a factual statement about ongoing clinical trials with trial registration numbers.
